content: Pregnant women are particularly susceptible to malaria, and the infection can lead to harmful outcomes for the fetus. Therefore, it is crucial to identify antimalarial treatments that are both safe and effective for use during pregnancy. A systematic review was conducted to compare the efficacy of various drug regimens for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in pregnant women. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials. The search for relevant studies was extensive, covering multiple databases such as the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and others, up to February 2008. Researchers also reached out to experts, organizations, and pharmaceutical companies to identify additional data. The review included 10 trials involving a total of 1,805 participants. Two of these trials were quasi-randomized, and seven did not adequately describe their methods for allocation concealment. All trials adjusted their treatment failure rates to exclude new infections. One trial demonstrated that the combination of artesunate and mefloquine resulted in significantly fewer treatment failures by day 63 compared to quinine (risk ratio [RR] 0.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 0.38; 106 participants). Another trial showed that artesunate combined with atovaquone-proguanil also led to fewer treatment failures by day 63 compared to quinine (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.57; 80 participants). In a separate trial, amodiaquine was found to be more effective than chloroquine in reducing treatment failures by day 28 (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.46; 420 participants). Additionally, the combination of amodiaquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine was significantly more effective than chloroquine alone (RR 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.26; 418 participants). Another trial compared sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine alone to combination therapies. It found that artesunate combined with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine reduced treatment failures at delivery or by day 40 (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.59; 79 participants). Similarly, azithromycin combined with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine was more effective than sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine alone (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.76; 82 participants). The authors concluded that while some combination therapies appear to be effective in treating malaria during pregnancy, the available data are limited. Furthermore, there is insufficient safety data to make definitive recommendations regarding the use of these treatments in pregnant women.
